Wieruszow Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Wieruszów, Poland

Not demolished. Wieruszów, a private town established in 1368, saw Jewish settlement from the early 17th century; an autonomous kehilla formed in 1810, with a synagogue following in 1850. Population reached 36% (1,587) by 1897, growing to about 2,400 before WWII, supported by a Jewish girls' school and (from 1917) kindergarten. On September 2, 1939, Germans massacred 21 Jews accused of defending a bridge over the Prosna River; an October 1941 ghetto's August 26, 1942 liquidation deported most residents to Auschwitz-Birkenau, while 86 elderly and sick people unable to travel were killed that same night at the town's mikveh. This cemetery, dated variously to the 17th or 18th century, received burials until before 1945. German forces used matzevot to pave sidewalks and the courtyard of a Gestapo headquarters; postwar recovery efforts returned several 19th-20th century tombstones to the site. It holds a combined mass grave of 107 people - 21 from Podzamcze shot early in the war, and the 86 mikveh massacre victims - marked by a plaque funded by Abram Majerowicz.
